- The [coordination recipes](coordination.qmd): `Lock`, `RLock`, `BoundedSemaphore`, `throttle`, `barrier`, `Averager` and `memoize_stampede`.
- [Tags](../recipes/invalidating-groups.qmd#option-2-tags) with `evict(tag)`, and `eviction_policy='none'`.
- The queue calls `push`, `pull`, `peek` and `peekitem` on `Cache` (see [Work queues](../recipes/work-queues.qmd)).

Tags and the eviction policy changed the on-disk format. 0.2.3 refuses a cache made by 0.1.2; since 0.3.5 such a cache opens in a versioned subdirectory instead, and `remove_old_formats()` cleans up the old one (see [Upgrading across a format change](../recipes/upgrading.qmd)).

### Done: Windows (0.3.5)

0.3.5 adds Windows on x86_64, with wheels for all four Pythons. Everything but the fork guarantees works the same there; [Getting started](getting-started.qmd#windows) lists what differs. Nothing changed on disk.

### Done: upgrades across a format change (0.3.5)

A release that meets a cache in another on-disk format opens a cache of its own in a versioned subdirectory and logs a warning, instead of refusing to open, so old and new workers keep running side by side during a deploy. `remove_old_formats()` cleans up the old cache once its workers are gone. See [Upgrading across a format change](../recipes/upgrading.qmd).

### Next

In roughly this order:

| What | What it delivers |
|---|---|
| **Django cache backend** | A diskcache-oxide backend for Django's cache framework, tested against Django's own cache test suite. It's a big job, so it gets a phase of its own. |
| **Free-threaded performance** | Make throughput scale with threads on 3.14t and 3.15t. Today a cached read spends about 60% of its time in one system call SQLite makes for its shared-memory lock, and that's the first target. |
| **`AsyncCache`** | An async API for asyncio frameworks that can't slow down the sync one, including `transact_async()`. It starts as an experiment and ships only if it earns its place; if it doesn't, this page will say why. |
| **Network server** | Stage 3, above. Speculative, and a separate product if it happens. |

### Decided against, and why

- **Least-recently-used and least-frequently-used eviction.** diskcache implements them by writing to the database on every `get`. Reads that never write are what let many processes read at once without queueing, so these stay out unless a design keeps reads write-free. Least-recently-stored stays the default, and `eviction_policy='none'` turns eviction off.
- **`Deque` and `Index`, until someone asks.** If you need one, open an issue. An `Index` is only as general as the key types, and both default to a temporary directory, which diskcache-oxide doesn't do.
- **`disk=` and `Disk` subclasses.** A Python class on every read and write would undo the Rust engine; `serializer=` and `register_type()` cover what people used them for.
- **Pickled keys.** Keys are never pickled, so listing keys never runs pickle and a key's identity doesn't depend on pickle's bytes.
- **`read=True` and `read()`** (streaming a file in and out). Folded into the large-file cache idea below.
- **Persisted statistics.** `stats()` counts per process, in memory, because diskcache's persisted counters make every `get` a write.

## Further out

Ideas being considered, not yet committed to:

- **Expiry that's exact everywhere.** Lookups already treat an expired entry as gone at the moment it expires. The plan is to make `len()` and iteration do the same, and move the physical cleanup to a small background sweeper written in Rust, coordinated across processes so eight workers don't all sweep at once.
- **A large-file cache**, handing out an open file rather than a path, which is where diskcache's `read=True` would fit.
- **Encryption at rest**, if a real need appears: SQLCipher for the database, authenticated encryption for spill files.

## Non-goals

- Reading existing diskcache directories. diskcache-oxide uses its own on-disk format, so caches start cold when you switch.
- A module named `diskcache` (it would collide with the real package).
- diskcache's own `DjangoCache` class. A Django backend of diskcache-oxide's own is planned, above.
- Python older than 3.14.



## Core Features

### Serialization

A cache has a quiet second job: it's a program that reads bytes it didn't write, left on disk by whatever process got there first. That makes the serializer the most security-relevant piece of the whole library, and it has three jobs. What goes into the cache should come out as exactly what you put in. Encoding and decoding should be fast, because they happen on every call. And reading the cache should never run code that someone else left there. diskcache's default, pickle, does the first two well and fails the third by design: unpickling runs whatever the bytes tell it to. diskcache-oxide gets all three, and pickle becomes something you opt into, one cache at a time.

## Two formats

Each cache picks a structured format with `serializer=`:

```python
cache = Cache('/var/cache/my-app')                       # msgpack, the default
readable = Cache('/var/cache/my-app-json', serializer='json')
```

- **msgpack** (the default) is compact and fast. On a 450 KB page-cache entry it's about 25× faster than tagged JSON, and it stores nested `bytes` without base64.
- **json** is human-readable: open `diskcache-oxide.sqlite` in any SQLite browser and read your values. It uses `serde_json` with exact float round-tripping. Keys aren't JSON: `str` keys show as text, and keys of other types as a short binary encoding (see [Keys and tags](#keys-and-tags)).

Plain `str` and `bytes` values skip both and are stored raw. Every row records how it was encoded, so if you change a cache's `serializer`, existing entries stay readable.

Everything stored as a value goes through the same encoder: what you pass to `set()`, `add()` and `push()`, and what a `memoize`d function returns.

## Exact types

JSON turns tuples into lists and can't store sets, datetimes, NaN, very large ints, or dicts with non-`str` keys. msgpack has some of the same gaps. The usual answer is to coerce quietly and let the bug show up later.

diskcache-oxide's encoder, written in Rust, notices anything its format would change and tags it instead, so it decodes back to the same type:

| Python value | Comes back as |
|---|---|
| `tuple` | a `tuple`, not a list |
| `set` | a `set` |
| `frozenset` | a `frozenset` |
| `datetime.datetime` | a `datetime`, with its timezone and microseconds |
| `datetime.date` | a `date` |
| `decimal.Decimal` | a `Decimal`, exact |
| `int` wider than 64 bits | the same int |
| `float('nan')`, `inf`, `-inf` | the same float |
| `bytes` nested in a container | `bytes` |
| `dict` with `int` (or other non-`str`) keys | the same keys |

```python
import datetime

cache.set('record', {
    'created': datetime.datetime.now(datetime.UTC),
    'point': (37.77, -122.42),
    'ids': {101, 102},
    'big': 2**128,
    'by_id': {1: 'one', 2: 'two'},
})

record = cache.get('record')
assert isinstance(record['point'], tuple)
assert record['by_id'][1] == 'one'
```

User data can't be mistaken for a tag: a dict that happens to look like one is escaped on the way in and decoded as an ordinary dict on the way out.

## What isn't stored

A value that neither format can represent exactly, such as an instance of your own class, raises `TypeError` at `set()`:

```python
cache.set('service', MyService())
# TypeError: values of type MyService can't be stored without pickle (only exact built-in types round-trip)
```

Only exact built-in types count. A subclass of `dict` or `str` isn't stored as its base type, because it wouldn't come back as the class you stored. Failing at `set()` time means you find out where the value was created, not three requests later when something reads it. For a type of your own, or one from a library, [register it](#your-own-types).

A `memoize`d function that returns such a value raises the same `TypeError`, after the function has run, when the result is stored. Nothing is cached, so the next call runs it again and raises again. Register the type, or have the function return something storable.

## Your own types

Most of what an app stores that isn't a built-in is a type it doesn't own: a bson `ObjectId` inside a session dict, a namedtuple a library hands back, the `str` subclass a Markdown renderer returns. Converting those by hand at every call site works, but it's the kind of code that drifts. Instead, tell the codec once how to store the type:

```python
from bson import ObjectId
import diskcache_oxide

diskcache_oxide.register_type(ObjectId, name='bson.ObjectId', encode=str, decode=ObjectId)

cache.set('session', {'id': ObjectId(), 'user': ObjectId()})
cache.get('session')['id']   # an ObjectId again
```

`encode` turns an instance into a value the codec can already store, built-ins or other registered types, nested as deep as you like. `decode` turns that value back into an instance. The registration is process-wide, so make it at import time, in every process that opens the directory.

A dataclass needs only a name. Its `init=True` fields are read straight off the instance, with no intermediate dict, and on the way out it's rebuilt with `cls(**fields)`, so defaults and `__post_init__` still run:

```python
@dataclasses.dataclass
class Episode:
    id: int
    title: str
    published: datetime.datetime | None = None

diskcache_oxide.register_type(Episode, name='tp.Episode')
cache.set('episode:491', Episode(491, 'Rust and Python'))
```

The write path skips `dataclasses.asdict()`, which deep-copies: on a 20-field dataclass a `set()` goes from about 23 µs to 18. A read still builds one keyword dict and calls the constructor, so it saves almost nothing (4.0 µs against 3.8), and that's fine: a cache is mostly reads, and what you gain is the call sites.

What the registry guarantees:

- **Nothing is imported by name.** A registered value is stored as `{"$t:bson.ObjectId": "..."}`, and a reader looks that name up in its own registry. A process that hasn't registered it gets `ForeignValueError`, and the row stays for one that has. That is the whole difference from pickle.
- **The name is yours.** Rename or move the class and the stored rows still read, because the tag is the name you chose, not the class's path.
- **Lookup is by exact type.** A subclass of a registered class is its own registration. The codec's own types (`str`, `dict`, `datetime` and the rest) can't be registered, since their wire form is a contract across versions; their subclasses can, which is how a namedtuple or a `str` subclass gets in.
- **A registered type is never pickled**, even on a cache with `pickle=True`. Once the encoder has used a registration for any part of a value, that value is stored through it or `set()` raises: if its `encode` raises, or returns something the codec can't store. You registered it to stay off pickle, and a silent fallback would hide the bug.
- **Last registration wins**, by class and by name, so a module that a dev server reloads can register its new class object again.
- **A decode function's errors are classified as a pickle hook's would be.** A `Timeout` or `OSError` raises with the row kept (a miss under `durable=True`). An error about the row, such as a `TypeError` from a dataclass row written before a field was removed, becomes `CorruptValueError` with yours as `__cause__`, and `on_decode_error='miss'` deletes that row so the writer replaces it. Decode runs while the cache holds a connection, as unpickling does, so a slow `decode` delays forks and checkpoints for as long as it runs; one that re-enters the cache is fine.

A cache that needs a different encoding of a type than the rest of the process gets its own registry, consulted before the global one:

```python
reg = diskcache_oxide.TypeRegistry()
reg.register(ObjectId, name='bson.ObjectId', encode=lambda o: o.binary, decode=ObjectId)
cache = Cache('/var/cache/my-app-binary-ids', types=reg)
```

Two processes with different registrations on one directory write rows the other can't read, the same way two processes with different `serializer=` settings would. Register at import time, the same way everywhere.

## Why pickle is off by default

- **Unpickling runs code.** Anyone who can write to the cache directory, including a compromised neighbor process or a shared volume, can make every reader run arbitrary Python.
- **Pickle hides mistakes.** Database sessions, open files and other objects that were never meant to be cached get pickled without complaint and fail later in confusing ways.

## Opting in to pickle

When you really do need to cache arbitrary objects, turn pickle on for that cache. It's used only for values the structured format can't represent; everything else is still stored as msgpack or JSON.

```python
objects = Cache('/var/cache/my-app-objects', pickle=True)
objects.set('service', MyService())
```

A good habit is to give pickled values their own cache directory, and keep everything else in a cache without pickle.

## Reading safely: `UnsafeValueError`

Several processes can open one directory with different settings. A handle opened without `pickle=True` never unpickles. If it reads a value that a `pickle=True` handle stored, it raises `diskcache_oxide.UnsafeValueError` (a `TypeError` subclass) and leaves the row in place, so the `pickle=True` handle can still read it.

A value whose stored bytes can't be decoded at all raises `CorruptValueError` (a `ValueError` subclass).

## Keys and tags

Keys follow stricter rules than values, because a key has to be compared, sorted and found as well as read back. They never go through `serializer=`, `pickle=` or the type registry. A key can be:

- `str`, `bytes`, `bool` or `None`
- an `int` that fits in 64 bits
- a `float`, except NaN, which raises `ValueError` because it isn't equal to itself
- a `tuple` of any of these, nested up to 32 deep

```python
cache.set(('episode', 491, 'transcript'), text)
cache.set(b'\x9f\x02', blob)
cache.set(42, 'the answer')
```

Anything else raises `TypeError`, even on a `pickle=True` cache: a `list`, a `dict`, a `bytearray`, an object, a registered type, and subclasses such as an `IntEnum`, a `StrEnum` or a namedtuple. If your key is an enum member, use its `.value`; if it's a namedtuple, pass `tuple(point)`.

Keys compare by exact type, so `1`, `1.0` and `True` are three different keys. Python's `==` says they're equal, and diskcache treats `1` and `1.0` as one key, so code that mixes them finds nothing where it expected a hit. The exception is `-0.0`, which is the same key as `0.0`, as it is in a dict.

A `str` key is stored as plain text. Every other key is stored in a compact binary encoding that sorts the way the values do, which is why `iterkeys()` can walk them in order: every `str` key first, then `None`, the bools, ints, floats, bytes and tuples, each group sorted. `iterkeys(prefix=...)` matches `str` keys only, so if you plan to list or delete a group of keys by prefix, make them strings (`'user:42:profile'`, not `('user', 42, 'profile')`).

A `memoize`d function's key is a tuple built from its name and its arguments, so every argument it's called with must be one of these types. A call with a list or an object raises `TypeError` before the function runs. Leave arguments like a database connection out of the key with `ignore=`.

Tags, from `set(..., tag=...)` and `memoize(tag=...)`, follow the same rules as keys and are stored the same way. `evict(1)` removes entries tagged `1` and leaves the ones tagged `1.0` or `True`.


### NullCache

Sooner or later you need to turn caching off. In tests, so each one starts clean. In local development, so you see your change instead of yesterday's. In production, at the worst possible moment, while you chase a bug that might be a stale entry and might not. Without help, that means `if cache is not None:` around every call, or a hand-written fake that drifts a little further from the real API with every release.

`NullCache` is a cache that's switched off. It has the same methods and signatures as `Cache`, so swapping one for the other is a one-line change, and the code that uses it never knows.

```python
from diskcache_oxide import Cache, CacheLike, NullCache

def make_cache(settings) -> CacheLike:
    if settings.cache_enabled:
        return Cache(settings.cache_dir)
    return NullCache()
```

## One rule

> **A `NullCache` behaves like a real cache in which every entry expires the instant it's written and is swept straight away.**

Every row of this table follows from that sentence, so you never have to guess, and once it clicks you never have to look it up again:

| Call | Result | Because |
|---|---|---|
| `get(key, default)` | `default` | the entry already expired |
| `get(key, tag=True)` | `(default, None)` | the entry and its tag already expired |
| `cache[key]` | raises `KeyError` | the entry already expired |
| `set(...)` | `True` | the write succeeded, then expired |
| a `@cache.memoize()` function | runs on every call | every stored result already expired |
| `add(...)` | `True` | the key was absent, so the add succeeded |
| `incr(key, delta, default)` | `default + delta` | it starts from the default each time; `KeyError` if `default=None` |
| `delete`, `touch`, `key in cache` | `False` | there's nothing there |
| `pop(key, default)` | `default` | there's nothing there |
| `push(value, ...)` | the first key a queue gets | the item expired the instant it was written |
| `pull()`, `peek()` | the default | the queue is empty; never forwarded to `invalidate=` |
| `peekitem()` | raises `KeyError` | it's empty |
| `len(cache)`, `cache.volume()` | `0` | it's empty and uses no disk |
| `expire()`, `clear()`, `cull()`, `evict(tag)` | `0` | nothing to remove |
| iteration, `iterkeys()`, `reversed(cache)` | nothing | it's empty |
| `stats()`, `check()` | `(0, 0)`, `[]` | nothing is looked up or stored |
| `remove_old_formats()` | `[]` | there's no directory to clean up |
| `bool(cache)`, `cache.enabled` | `False` | caching is off |

The constructor accepts the same arguments as `Cache` and ignores them, and the directory is optional. Bad arguments still raise as they would on `Cache` (a list as a key or a tag, `expire=True`, `side='middle'` on a queue call), and a memoized function's arguments are still checked as keys, so a call that would raise on a real cache raises here too. Values are the exception. A `NullCache` never encodes them, so `set()` accepts a value a real cache would refuse with `TypeError` (see [Serialization](serialization.qmd#what-isnt-stored)), and so does a memoized function that returns one. A test suite that runs only against a `NullCache` won't catch those.

### Watch `add()`

The rule means `add()` always succeeds on a `NullCache`. If you use `add()` to claim a job so only one worker runs it, then with caching off every worker's claim succeeds and the job runs once per worker. That's harmless for idempotent work and wrong for work with side effects, like sending email. Keep claims like that on a cache that's never switched off.

`Cache(durable=True)` goes the other way: its `add()` returns `False` when a write fails, so a claim fails closed there and open here. Keep claims on a handle that isn't durable and handle its exceptions. See [A cache that can't take a request down](getting-started.qmd#a-cache-that-cant-take-a-request-down).

The [coordination recipes](coordination.qmd) won't run on a `NullCache` at all. `Lock`, `RLock`, `BoundedSemaphore`, `Averager`, `throttle` and `barrier` raise `TypeError`, because a lock that every caller holds at once is worse than no lock. `memoize_stampede` is a cache rather than a lock, so it runs on one the way `memoize` does, calling the function every time.

### Watch the queue calls

A queue on a `NullCache` is always empty. `push()` returns the key an empty queue's first item would get and stores nothing, so with caching off every job you push is lost, and `pull()` on the other side never sees it. Keep a [work queue](../recipes/work-queues.qmd) on a cache that's never switched off, as you would a claim.

## `if cache:` means "caching is on"

`bool(Cache(...))` is always True and `bool(NullCache())` is always False, and both have an `enabled` property. (In diskcache, an empty real cache is falsy, which makes this check unreliable.)

```python
if cache:
    log.info('Caching is on')
```

## Keep invalidating while caching is off: `invalidate=`

Turning caching off creates a trap. While it's off, your app keeps changing data, and the code that would have deleted the now-stale cache entries is talking to a `NullCache`. When you turn caching back on, the real cache serves the stale values.

`invalidate=` closes the trap. Give the `NullCache` the real cache, and it forwards the operations that *remove* data to it, while everything else stays switched off:

```python
real = Cache('/var/cache/my-app')
cache = NullCache(invalidate=real)

cache.set('user:42', profile)    # not cached
cache.get('user:42')             # None
cache.delete('user:42')          # deleted from the real cache
cache.pop('user:42')             # deleted from the real cache; returns the default
cache.clear()                    # clears the real cache
cache.evict('user:42')           # evicts the tag from the real cache
cache.iterkeys(prefix='user:')   # the real cache's keys, so list-then-delete still works
```

When caching comes back on, nothing you invalidated by removing it is waiting. That covers a memoized function too: `cache.delete(f.__cache_key__(42))` reaches the real cache, and so does `evict(tag)` for results stored with `memoize(tag=...)`.

The queue calls are never forwarded. `pull()` and `peek()` on a `NullCache(invalidate=real)` return the default and leave the real cache's queue alone, because a cache that's switched off must not consume real jobs.

Only removals are forwarded, so invalidating by *writing* is lost while caching is off. Overwriting the stale value with a fresh `set`, or bumping a version key with `incr` so readers build a new key, does nothing, and the old value is served once caching is back on:

```python
cache = NullCache(invalidate=real)   # real holds 'user:42' = old_profile, and 'users:version' = 3

cache.set('user:42', new_profile)    # dropped: real still has old_profile
cache.incr('users:version')          # dropped: still 3, so readers keep reading the old keys
```

If your app invalidates that way, delete the entry instead (or as well), or `clear()` the real cache when you turn caching back on.

## `CacheLike`

`CacheLike` is a `typing.Protocol` that both `Cache` and `NullCache` satisfy. Annotate with it and ty or pyright will accept either:

```python
from diskcache_oxide import CacheLike

def load_user(user_id: str, cache: CacheLike) -> dict:
    if (user := cache.get(f'user:{user_id}')) is not None:
        return user
    user = db.load_user(user_id)
    cache.set(f'user:{user_id}', user, expire=300)
    return user
```

It covers everything the two share: the reads and writes with their `tag=` and `retry=` options, `memoize`, `evict`, the maintenance calls, `stats`, `check` and `reset`, iteration, and the `durable` and `eviction_policy` attributes. A test in diskcache-oxide's own suite checks that `Cache`, `NullCache` and `CacheLike` keep identical public signatures, so they can't drift apart.

## `transact()` and `TransactionalCacheLike`

`NullCache.transact()` is a no-op context manager that yields the `NullCache`, so code written as `with cache.transact() as tx:` runs unchanged with caching off. There's nothing to commit or roll back. It accepts `retry=` as `Cache.transact()` does, and a keyword-only `key=`, which it ignores.

With `invalidate=`, it never opens a transaction on the real cache: a switched-off cache must never take a write lock or raise `Timeout`. So removals forwarded inside the block land at once, and an exception in the block doesn't undo them.

`CacheLike` leaves out `transact()` and the queue calls, because a `FanoutCache` satisfies it too: its `transact` takes a key, and it has no queue calls. To accept a `Cache` or a `NullCache` and call `transact()`, `push`, `pull`, `peek` or `peekitem`, annotate with `TransactionalCacheLike`, which adds them. See [Transactions](transactions.qmd#typing-transactionalcachelike). A [`FanoutCache`](fanoutcache.qmd)'s `transact` takes a key, so for code that accepts a `FanoutCache` or a `NullCache` use `ShardedCacheLike` instead (see [Typing](fanoutcache.qmd#typing)); the `key=` a `NullCache` ignores is what lets it satisfy both.


### Caches: named caches

Every app with two caches eventually grows a file called something like `cache_service.py`. It maps names to directories, opens each cache once and hands out the same object afterwards, carries on with caching switched off when a directory can't be opened, lets you turn one off for a load test, and feeds counts and sizes to an admin page. It's the same file in every app, written slightly differently each time. `Caches` is that file, so you don't have to write it again.

```python
from diskcache_oxide import Caches

caches = Caches('/var/cache/my-app', timeout=1.0, on_decode_error='miss')
caches.register('general')
caches.register('pages', size_limit=2 * 2**30)

caches['general'].set('greeting', 'hello')
caches['pages'].get('/about')
```

Settings passed to `Caches` apply to every cache, and `register` can override them for one. Each cache lives in a directory named after it under the base directory, unless you pass `directory=`.

One setting works differently here: a function passed as `on_decode_error` is called as `report(name, key, exc)`, with the cache's name first, so one reporter can serve every cache. (On a plain `Cache` it's `report(key, exc)`.) A function that doesn't take three arguments is rejected when you create the registry or register the cache.

## Lookups

A cache opens on its first lookup, and every lookup after that returns the same object. A lookup is a single dict read with no lock, so it's fine to do on every request rather than keeping your own references. Lookups are safe from any thread, on free-threaded Python too, and in a child process after a fork.

`Caches` is generic in its names. Give it a `Literal` and a misspelled name becomes a type error:

```python
from typing import Literal

CacheName = Literal['general', 'pages']
caches: Caches[CacheName] = Caches('/var/cache/my-app')
caches['genral']  # ty: invalid argument
```

## When a cache can't open

A cache can fail to open: a permissions problem, a disk that went away, a directory that holds the other kind of cache, or another process holding the lock for longer than `timeout`. (A cache in another on-disk format isn't one of them: it opens in its versioned subdirectory, below.) A lookup then returns a [NullCache](null-cache.qmd) instead of raising, so the request carries on without the cache. The error goes to `on_open_error(name, exc)`, which logs it at `ERROR` on the `diskcache_oxide` logger by default. Pass your own function to send it to Sentry or your logging setup.

The failure is remembered for `retry_open_after` seconds (10 by default), so a broken cache costs one failed open every 10 seconds, not one per request, and the lookup after that tries again. A cache that recovers is picked up without a restart. Under load, several threads may make that retry at the same moment, and each one that fails reports it.

`MemoryError` isn't an open failure, so it raises from the lookup, as it would from `Cache(...)`. That includes SQLite running out of memory while opening (`SQLITE_NOMEM`), which used to be an `OSError` and got a `NullCache`.

A `Timeout` at open means busy, not broken: another process holding the lock, or a first lookup that collided with a fork. It's remembered for at most 1 second, and the default report is a `WARNING` with no traceback. A custom `on_open_error` still gets the exception. Lookups of a cache that's already open never touch any of this.

A bad *setting* (`size_limit=True`, `serializer='yaml'`) is a bug, not an outage, so it raises on lookup instead. What each open error means, and the fix, is in [Errors and what to do about them](errors.qmd).

### After an upgrade that changes the format

When a release changes the on-disk format, a registered cache whose directory holds the old format opens a new, empty cache in the subdirectory `diskcache-oxide-format-N` and logs a warning, as a plain `Cache` does: no `NullCache`, no retry, and `on_open_error` isn't called. `caches.directory(name)` still gives the registered directory, and the handle's `directory` says where the cache really is. Once the old workers are gone, `caches.remove_old_formats()` removes every registered cache's old files and returns what it removed, by name. It doesn't check for old workers: read [Upgrading across a format change](../recipes/upgrading.qmd) before you call it.

## Sharded caches

Pass `shards=` to `register` to open a [`FanoutCache`](fanoutcache.qmd) instead of a `Cache`. It takes the same settings, and `max_connections` is then a total across the shards.

```python
caches.register('rate_limits', shards=8)
caches.fanout('rate_limits').incr('ip:203.0.113.7')
```

A plain cache is read with `caches[name]` and a sharded one with `caches.fanout(name)`, typed `FanoutCache | NullCache`, because its `transact` takes a key. Reading a name the wrong way raises `TypeError`. Passing `shards` at all picks the kind, even `shards=None`, so a config file that writes `shards: null` for "none" would register a `FanoutCache`: leave it out. A directory that holds the other kind of cache fails to open with `LayoutMismatchError`, and the lookup returns a `NullCache` like any failed open.

A sharded cache keeps the shard count it was created with. `register('rate_limits', shards=16)` on a folder that already has 8 shards opens it with 8, logs a `WARNING` saying so and how to apply 16, and logs one `ERROR` per process so an error tracker hears of it. Every process then routes keys by the same count, so a deploy that changes `shards=` keeps working while old and new workers overlap. The registered count applies only to a new folder: to change it, delete the folder with every worker stopped, for example at deploy. A folder deleted while old workers still run is re-created by whichever process opens it first, with that process's count. One case is still a `NullCache`: a `size_limit` or `max_connections` that fits the registered count but is too small to split over the folder's count (at least one connection and 1 MiB a shard) fails with `LayoutMismatchError` naming both counts. A setting that's wrong for the registered count itself still raises `ValueError` from the lookup, as any bad setting does. A direct `FanoutCache(path, shards=16)` on that folder opens with 8 too, and logs its own `WARNING`. Pass `raise_on_mismatch=True`, to `register()` or to `FanoutCache`, to make another count an error instead: in the registry that's an open failure, so the lookup returns a reported `NullCache`. Everything else on this page (`disable`, `stats`, `clear`, `expire_all`, `close_all`) works the same for both kinds.

## Switching caches off

```python
caches.disable('pages')   # later lookups return NullCache(invalidate=real)
caches.enable('pages')
caches.enabled('pages')   # False while it's off
```

While a cache is disabled, its lookups return `NullCache(invalidate=real)`: reads miss and writes are dropped, but `delete` and `clear` still reach the real cache, so entries you invalidate by removing them aren't served stale when it comes back on. Invalidating by writing doesn't survive: an overwriting `set` or a version-bump `incr` is dropped like any other write, and the old value is served again (see [Keep invalidating while caching is off](null-cache.qmd#keep-invalidating-while-caching-is-off-invalidate)). Switches only change later lookups. Code that already holds the real `Cache` keeps using it, so set them at startup, before you hand caches out.

If your app has its own names for what it caches (Talk Python calls them purposes), map them onto registered caches in your own code. It's a few lines:

```python
PURPOSES = {'rss_feed': 'general', 'episode_html': 'episodes'}
off = {'rss_feed'}  # from your settings file

def cache_for(purpose: str) -> CacheLike:
    real = caches[PURPOSES[purpose]]
    return NullCache(invalidate=real) if purpose in off else real
```

Build the wrapper on each call rather than memoizing it: `caches[...]` is already cheap, and a memoized `NullCache(invalidate=...)` wrapped around a cache that had failed to open would never pick up its recovery.

## `memoize` on a registered cache

`@caches['episodes'].memoize()` does the lookup once, when the module is imported, and the decorated function keeps whatever came back. If the cache couldn't open at that moment, the function holds a `NullCache` and runs uncached until the process restarts, even after the cache recovers. `disable('episodes')` never reaches it either, because switches only change later lookups.

If that matters to you, look the cache up on each call instead. A small decorator does it:

```python
import functools

def memoized(name: str, **options):
    def decorator(func):
        @functools.wraps(func)
        def wrapper(*args, **kwargs):
            return caches[name].memoize(**options)(func)(*args, **kwargs)
        return wrapper
    return decorator

@memoized('episodes', expire=600)
def episode(number: int) -> dict:
    return load_episode(number)
```

It stores under the same keys as `@caches['episodes'].memoize(expire=600)` would, and it follows recovery and the switches. Building the wrapper on every call added about 2 µs per call when we measured it. To forget one result, build the key the same way: `caches['episodes'].delete(caches['episodes'].memoize()(episode.__wrapped__).__cache_key__(42))`.

## Locks, claims and queues

Give coordination its own registered cache, with settings that suit it:

```python
caches = Caches('/var/cache/my-app', timeout=1.0, durable=True)
caches.register('pages')
caches.register('locks', durable=False, eviction_policy='none')
```

The [coordination recipes](coordination.qmd) (`Lock`, `RLock`, `BoundedSemaphore`, `throttle`, `barrier`, `Averager`) raise `TypeError` on a `durable=True` cache, since a dropped `delete` would leave a lock held, so a registry whose defaults include `durable=True` needs `durable=False` on this one. `eviction_policy='none'` stops a size-limit eviction from removing a lock or a claim that's still live. Give those entries an `expire` instead.

The recipes also raise `TypeError` on a `NullCache`, so while `locks` is disabled or can't open, `Lock(caches['locks'], ...)` raises where it would otherwise have taken the lock. That's on purpose: a lock that every caller holds at once is worse than an error. Catch it where losing the lock means skipping the work. The decorators `@throttle(...)` and `@barrier(...)` check their cache when they decorate, so one applied to `caches['locks']` at import time raises at import if that cache can't open.

The [queue calls](../recipes/work-queues.qmd) (`push`, `pull`, `peek`, `peekitem`) are on `caches[name]`, so register a queue's cache without `shards=`: a `FanoutCache` has no queue calls. While that cache is disabled or can't open, `push` returns a key and stores nothing, and the job is gone. If a lost job matters, check `caches['jobs'].enabled` before you push, or open the queue's cache with `Cache(...)` directly so that a failure raises.

## Admin and shutdown

```python
caches.stats()                      # {name: CacheStats(name, directory, enabled, count, volume, error)}
caches.clear('pages', timeout=10)   # works on a disabled cache too
caches.expire_all(timeout=10)       # {name: removed, or None if it failed}
caches.close_all()                  # at shutdown; `with Caches(...) as caches:` does it too
```

- `stats()` opens every registered cache and never raises: a cache that can't be read has its `error` set.
- Hit and miss counts come from each cache's own `stats()`: `caches['pages'].stats()` turns counting on for this process, and later calls return `(hits, misses)` for this process's lookups. A disabled cache, or one that couldn't open, returns `(0, 0)`.
- `clear(name)` raises if the cache can't be opened, so an admin page doesn't report "0 cleared" for a failure.
- `expire_all()` runs every cache, logging and reporting `None` for one that fails. Run it from a scheduled job rather than inside a request: a large expire takes seconds.
- Maintenance calls hold the write lock once per chunk, so give them a longer `timeout=` than the request path's.

## Coming from your own diskcache wrapper

Apps that run diskcache in production tend to grow the same wrapper around it: a class that turns errors into misses, a null cache for turning caching off, and a module that creates, lists and maintains the app's caches. Talk Python's, for one, are a `DurableCache` class and a `cache_service` module, and the left column uses their names. Each piece now has a home in the library:

| A typical wrapper | diskcache-oxide |
|---|---|
| `bool()` is always True | `Cache` is always truthy (D-009); `NullCache` is falsy |
| `CacheProtocol` | `CacheLike` |
| `NullCache`, `PerfTestNullCache` | `NullCache`, and `NullCache(invalidate=real)` |
| `get` that logs, deletes and misses on any error | `Cache(on_decode_error='miss')` or a reporting function ([details](getting-started.qmd#values-that-cant-be-read)) |
| A cache that can't take a request down | `Caches(base_dir, durable=True)`, which also covers `set`, whose failures such a wrapper usually raises ([details](getting-started.qmd#a-cache-that-cant-take-a-request-down)) |
| `create_cache(name, size_limit)` | `caches.register(name, size_limit=...)`, then `caches[name]` |
| `timeout=1.0` on every open | `Caches(base_dir, timeout=1.0)` |
| A `NullCache` when opening fails | the same, reported through `on_open_error` and retried after 10 s |
| `get_all_caches()`, `clear_*()`, `close_all_caches()` | `caches.stats()`, `caches.clear(name, timeout=...)`, `caches.close_all()` |
| A separate maintenance handle with a 10 s timeout | `timeout=` on `clear()`, `expire()` and `cull()` |
| Hourly `expire_all_caches()` inside `create_cache` | `caches.expire_all()` from a scheduled job |

The library's self-healing read is safer than the wrapper's in three ways:

- **It deletes only what failed.** The wrapper's `get`-then-`delete` can remove a fresh value another process wrote in between. The library deletes exactly the stored version it couldn't read.
- **It never waits to clean up.** If the write lock is busy, the bad row stays and a later read tries again.
- **It doesn't hide outages.** The wrapper catches every exception, so a lock `Timeout` also became a silent miss. In the library, `Timeout`, I/O errors and `MemoryError` still raise by default, and so does reading a pickled value from a cache without `pickle=True`, which is a configuration mistake. `durable=True` is how you choose a miss for an outage, and it counts each one and logs them, at most once a minute, rather than staying silent; `MemoryError` and that mistake raise regardless.

What stays in the app: reading its settings file and environment variables (pass the result as `base_dir`), its purposes and their on/off flags, descriptions for the admin page, and wiring the reporting functions to Sentry or logbook.


### FanoutCache: sharded caches

A plain `Cache` has one write lock per database file, which makes it a shop with one checkout lane: readers walk straight through, but every writer queues, and eight worker processes that all bump counters are eight carts in one lane. A `FanoutCache` opens more lanes. It's one cache spread over several SQLite databases, called shards. Each key lives in exactly one shard, chosen by a fixed hash of the key, so writes to different keys go to different files and stop queueing on one lock. It has the same methods as `Cache` for single keys, and it's one directory, shared by any number of threads and processes.

```python
from diskcache_oxide import FanoutCache

cache = FanoutCache('/var/cache/my-app-rate-limits', shards=8)

cache.set('ip:203.0.113.7', 1, expire=60)
cache.incr('ip:203.0.113.7')
cache.shard_of('ip:203.0.113.7')   # 0 to 7, the same in every process and every release
```

## Should you use it?

Use `FanoutCache` when **several processes write to the same cache**. Use a plain [`Cache`](getting-started.qmd) when they don't. The numbers come from the benchmark in the repository (`bench/fanout.py`, release builds, a 99:1 get:set mix with 1 KB values on a Mac with 18 cores):

| Processes | Plain `Cache` | `FanoutCache(shards=8)` | diskcache `FanoutCache(8)` |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 660k ops/s | 714k | 396k |
| 4 | 607k | 1,553k | 987k |
| 8 | 262k | 1,496k | 1,238k |

- **It removes the multi-process write-lock ceiling.** A plain `Cache` peaks at two processes and then falls, because the 1% of operations that are writes all queue on one database file's write lock. A `FanoutCache` keeps climbing and holds its rate: 5.7x a plain `Cache` at 8 processes, and 1.2x diskcache's `FanoutCache`. If your app runs a pre-forking server with a worker per core and writes often (counters, rate limits, job claims), this is the case it's for.
- **It does not yet make threads sharing one handle scale on free-threaded Python.** Four threads on one `FanoutCache` handle read no faster than, and on Linux slower than, four threads on a plain `Cache`, and well short of four separate handles. A larger `max_connections` helps but doesn't close the gap. This is a limit in what threads on one handle share, it's being worked on, and no numbers are promised here. If your concern is read throughput from many threads in one process, a `FanoutCache` doesn't fix it today.
- **On GIL builds, threads are flat for every diskcache-oxide cache,** as the GIL says they must be, and a `FanoutCache` is about 10 to 15% ahead of a plain `Cache` on that mix at one thread. It's well ahead of stock diskcache, which collapses as threads are added.
- **A single process with a few threads and few writes gains little.** You pay the cost of more files (below) for a benefit you won't see.

Single-key reads and writes cost the same as on `Cache` plus the hash, which is about the cost of one more string hash, while no transaction is open in the process (see `transact(key=)` below).

## The layout and the hash

A `FanoutCache` directory looks like this:

```
my-app-rate-limits/
  diskcache-oxide-fanout          the manifest
  000/diskcache-oxide.sqlite      shard 0
  001/diskcache-oxide.sqlite      shard 1
  ...
```

Each shard is an ordinary diskcache-oxide database. The manifest records the shard count and the hash. A key's shard is XXH3-64 (seed 0) of its type byte and its UTF-8 bytes, mapped onto the shard count. **That hash is part of the on-disk format and is frozen**: pinned by golden vectors in the test suite, so every process and every release sends a key to the same place. A future scheme would get a new format number, never a change in place.

Because the shard count decides where every key lives, it's recorded, and a different `shards=` never changes it. The cache opens with the count it has and logs a warning, once per process, instead of quietly losing data. Pass `raise_on_mismatch=True` to make it an error instead:

```python
FanoutCache('/var/cache/my-app-rate-limits', shards=16)
# WARNING: FanoutCache at /var/cache/my-app-rate-limits has 8 shards but shards=16 was asked for; using the 8 it has. ...

FanoutCache('/var/cache/my-app-rate-limits', shards=16, raise_on_mismatch=True)
# LayoutMismatchError: this FanoutCache has 8 shards but shards=16 was requested; changing the count needs a new directory
```

`shards=None` (the default) uses the stored count, or creates 8. Changing the count means a new directory. `raise_on_mismatch` covers the count only: a root in another on-disk format opens in its versioned subdirectory either way (below). Creating the manifest uses a hard link, so a filesystem without them (FAT, exFAT, SMB, some FUSE mounts) raises `OSError` saying so.

### Plain `Cache` and `FanoutCache` directories don't mix

A `Cache` opened on a `FanoutCache`'s directory, or on one of its shard directories, raises `LayoutMismatchError`, and so does a `FanoutCache` opened on a plain `Cache`'s directory. The refused open creates nothing, so a typo doesn't leave a directory that neither kind can open. `LayoutMismatchError` is both a `ValueError` and a `FormatMismatchError`. If a registry hits it, the lookup returns a [`NullCache`](null-cache.qmd) and reports it like any failed open. That holds for a shard directory in any on-disk format.

A root in another on-disk format, whether its manifest or any of its shards, opens as a whole in the root's `diskcache-oxide-format-N` subdirectory, a new root with its own shards and the count you ask for (or 8), and logs a warning, as a plain `Cache` does. One shard never moves on its own. `remove_old_formats()` removes the old root's shards, highest first, and its manifest last. See [Upgrading across a format change](../recipes/upgrading.qmd). A registry that meets another shard count than its registration's opens the folder with the count on disk and warns instead ([Caches](caches.qmd)).

## Choosing `shards` and `max_connections`

**`shards`** is 1 to 256. Eight is a good start: the benchmark's write scaling is already flat by 4 processes at 8 shards. More shards spread writes further but cost file descriptors (below) and give each shard a smaller share of `size_limit`. Pick it once, because it's permanent for the directory.

**`max_connections`** is the most SQLite connections the process opens for the whole `FanoutCache`, split across the shards (`max_connections // shards` each, with the first `max_connections % shards` getting one more). It must be at least `shards`, and the default is two per shard with a floor of 8 in all: 16 at the default 8 shards. With one per shard, threads sharing a handle waited for a shard's only connection and read 16-31% below a plain `Cache`; two gets 97-98% of the read rate of 32. SQLite's page caches for the whole cache are then about `16 × sqlite_cache_size` (16 MiB at the defaults, against a plain `Cache`'s 8). A busy shard only gets its share, so if a measurement shows one hot shard waiting for a connection, raise it. It doesn't matter across processes, since each process has its own connections.

**File descriptors.** Each connection holds its shard's database and WAL open, and each shard adds its `-shm` file and a pin. The descriptors inside the root stay within `2 × max_connections + 2 × shards`, however many threads you run: 48 at the defaults, measured at 32-34 with 64 threads on 3.14t. That's a ceiling, reached only when that many threads hit the same shards at once, since a shard opens its second connection only then, where stock diskcache's FanoutCache holds 264. `close()` leaves none. Opening needs about 4 per shard, so 256 shards need more than 1,024, Linux's usual default `ulimit -n`. If there aren't enough, opening raises `OSError` with `errno` `EMFILE`, and a message giving the shard count, the descriptors needed, the limit and how many are already open. A failed open leaves no descriptor behind.

**`size_limit`** is a total. Each shard gets `floor(size_limit / shards)` and culls on its own, and each needs at least 1 MiB, so the total must be at least `shards` MiB (`ValueError` otherwise). A new root with none given gets 1 GiB in all. `cache.size_limit` reads back the total (the sum of the shards' floored shares). A key that happens to land in a full shard evicts from that shard, even if the others have room.

## `shard_of` and `transact(key=)`

`cache.shard_of(key)` says which shard a key lives in. It's how you find out which keys can share a transaction.

`transact` on a `FanoutCache` is not stock's. Stock's takes every shard's lock, so one transaction stalls every writer in every process. Here it's a transaction on **one shard**, named by a key:

```python
with cache.transact(key='totals:2026-11') as tx:
    n = tx.get('totals:2026-11', 0)
    tx.set('totals:2026-11', n + 1)
```

- **Only that shard is locked.** Writes to other shards, from other threads and processes, carry on.
- **`key` is required and keyword-only.** A ported `with cache.transact():` raises `TypeError`, and so does `transact('k')`, so a key can't be mistaken for `retry`.
- **Other shards' keys are refused, reads included.** On the thread inside the block, a call for a key on any other shard raises `ValueError` naming both shards, through any handle on the same directory. Entering a second `transact` for a key on another shard is refused too. A nested `transact` for a key on the same shard joins the outer one. A read on another shard is refused because it would see a value the block's writes can't be atomic with, so a block that mixes shards is a mistake either way, and it's caught on the first call.
- **Whole-cache calls are refused too.** `len()`, `volume()`, iteration (`iter()`, `iterkeys()`, and `next()` on an iterator made before the block), `clear()`, `expire()`, `cull()`, `evict()`, `check()`, `reset()` and `checkpoint()` raise `ValueError` inside the block, since they would run inside the transaction on one shard and outside it on the rest. Inside the block, only keyed calls on the transaction's shard reach the cache. Call the others before or after it. `close()` isn't refused, since it never raises.
- Everything else is as in [Transactions](transactions.qmd): commit on exit, roll back on an exception, `retry=`, `TransactionBusy`, and `durable=True` still raising.

If you need related keys in one transaction, give them a shared prefix scheme and check with `shard_of` that they land together, or keep them in one value. There is no transaction across shards.

A `FanoutCache` isn't a `TransactionalCacheLike`, because its `transact` needs a key. It and `NullCache` are both [`ShardedCacheLike`](#typing).

## Maintenance: one budget, partial failures

`clear()`, `expire()`, `cull()` and `checkpoint()` run over every shard. Their `timeout=` (default: the handle's) bounds **the whole call**, not each shard. The handle's timeout also bounds opening, `len()` and `volume()` as one budget, and `close()` uses at most 1 s of it for checkpoints. A shard reached after the deadline still gets one try with no wait, so idle shards are always done.

A shard that fails doesn't stop the others. Afterwards the call raises the first failure's own type, so `except Timeout` works, with attributes saying how far it got:

```python
try:
    cache.clear(timeout=5)
except Timeout as exc:
    exc.failed_shards   # (3,): the indexes of the shards that failed
    exc.removed         # entries removed in all, including what a failed shard removed before it failed
```

`removed` is the total removed in all, including what a failed shard removed before it failed, except for `checkpoint()`, which has none; `checkpoint()` returns True only if every shard's log was reset. Writes made while a removal runs survive on every shard, as on `Cache`. `durable=True` doesn't swallow any of these.

## Timeouts on single keys

On a `FanoutCache`, diskcache silently turns a busy shard into a dropped write: `set` gives False after 10 ms. diskcache-oxide behaves as `Cache` does: a busy shard raises `Timeout` after `timeout` (60 seconds by default), and so do `cache[k]`, `cache[k] = v` and `del cache[k]`. If you want a miss instead, say so with [`durable=True`](getting-started.qmd#a-cache-that-cant-take-a-request-down), which also logs and counts the failures, with one report for the whole `FanoutCache`.

## Iteration order

`iter(cache)` yields every key once, shard 0 to the last, each shard in its insertion order. That is not the cache's insertion order, and not stock's, since the shards hold different keys. `iterkeys(prefix=, reverse=)` merges the shards into one sorted order, the same order a plain `Cache` gives, and holds no connection between yields. `reversed(cache)` walks the shards from the last to shard 0, each newest first. Neither is a snapshot: a concurrent write may or may not be seen, never twice.

## In a `Caches` registry

Pass `shards=` to `register` and the name opens a `FanoutCache`, with the same settings as any other cache:

```python
caches = Caches('/var/cache/my-app', timeout=1.0, durable=True)
caches.register('general')
caches.register('rate_limits', shards=8, max_connections=16)

caches['general'].get('greeting')
caches.fanout('rate_limits').incr('ip:203.0.113.7')
```

Plain caches are read with `caches[name]` and sharded ones with `caches.fanout(name)`, because their `transact` takes a key. Reading a name the wrong way raises `TypeError`. Passing `shards` at all is what picks the kind, so `shards=None` still registers a `FanoutCache`; leave it out for a plain cache. A failed open becomes a `NullCache`, `disable()`, `stats()`, `clear()` and `close_all()` work the same, and `fanout(name)` is typed `FanoutCache | NullCache`. See [Caches](caches.qmd).

## Typing

`ShardedCacheLike` is a protocol for "a `CacheLike` whose `transact` takes `key=`". Both `FanoutCache` and `NullCache` satisfy it, so code that works with either a sharded cache or a switched-off one can be annotated with it:

```python
from diskcache_oxide import ShardedCacheLike

def bump(cache: ShardedCacheLike, key: str) -> None:
    with cache.transact(key=key) as tx:
        tx.set(key, tx.get(key, 0) + 1)
```

## What `FanoutCache` doesn't have

`memoize`, `stats()`, `check()`, `reset()`, `reversed()`, pickling, `retry=`, tags and `evict(tag)` (which removes the tag from every shard) and `eviction_policy=` (every shard's) work as on `Cache`. The queue calls `push`, `pull`, `peek` and `peekitem` are on `Cache` only, because a queue spread over shards would have no order; keep a [work queue](../recipes/work-queues.qmd) in a plain `Cache`. diskcache's `cache()`, `deque()` and `index()` sub-collections and `read()`/`read=` aren't here either (see the [roadmap](roadmap.qmd)). `directory` is required and there's no `disk=`, as for `Cache`.

The constructor takes `shards` as a keyword: stock's `FanoutCache(path, 4)` means four shards, but here the second argument is `timeout`, so write `shards=4`.


### Transactions

Every write is already its own transaction, atomic across every thread and process using the directory. Sometimes one write at a time isn't enough. A request bumps a total, bumps a per-path counter and records when it happened, and a reader that sees two of those three has seen something that was never true. `transact()` groups several calls into one: they all commit together when the block exits, or none of them do.

```python
with cache.transact() as tx:
    tx.incr('requests')
    tx.incr(f'requests:{path}')
    tx.set('last_request', now)
```

That's also faster. Each commit costs a disk sync, so grouping writes pays for one instead of several: three counter bumps measured 79 µs one by one and 48 µs in one transaction.

## What the block does

- **Commit on exit, roll back on an exception.** If the block raises, none of its writes are kept, and the exception carries on as usual.
- **`tx` is the cache itself.** On the thread that entered the block, every call on that cache directory inside it runs in the transaction, whether you call it on `tx`, on `cache`, or on another `Cache` handle for the same directory. diskcache's `transact()` yields `None`, so code written for it keeps working.
- **The block reads its own writes.** Other threads and processes see nothing until it commits, and their writes to this directory wait for it, up to their own `timeout`. Keep blocks short.
- **Nesting joins the outer block.** A `transact()` inside another one on the same directory, on the same thread, joins the outer transaction instead of starting its own. As in diskcache, the inner block's exit commits nothing, and an exception you catch inside the outer block doesn't undo the inner block's writes. Only the outer block's exit commits.

```python
with cache.transact():
    cache.set('a', 1)
    try:
        with cache.transact():
            cache.set('b', 2)
            raise ValueError
    except ValueError:
        pass
# Both 'a' and 'b' are committed: the inner block had no savepoint of its own.
```

The object `transact()` returns is used once: entering it a second time, or while another thread is entering it, raises `RuntimeError`.

## Beginning one: `timeout` and `retry=`

Beginning a transaction takes the directory's write lock, and waits for it up to the cache's `timeout`, then raises `Timeout`, as a write does. With `retry=True` it keeps trying instead. Each attempt waits up to `timeout` with the interpreter released, and `Ctrl-C` is checked between attempts, so a `KeyboardInterrupt` gets through within one `timeout`.

```python
with cache.transact(retry=True) as tx:
    ...
```

### Two caches at once: `TransactionBusy`

Inside one cache's transaction, beginning a transaction on a second cache takes that cache's write lock if it's free. If another thread holds it, `transact()` raises `TransactionBusy` at once instead of waiting: that thread could be waiting for the lock you hold, and then neither would ever finish. `TransactionBusy` is a subclass of `Timeout`, so existing handlers still catch it, and `retry=True` never retries it, since trying again while you still hold the first lock can't help.

To use two caches in one block, always nest them in the same order everywhere in your app, and if `TransactionBusy` reaches you, leave the outer block and try the whole thing again.

## When a block doesn't commit

A `with` block never exits cleanly when its writes are gone. Its exit raises `TransactionAborted`, a `RuntimeError`, when the transaction didn't commit:

- an operation inside it failed in a way that left the transaction unusable (a full disk, an I/O error). Later writes in the block fail at once, and nothing in it commits;
- it was ended from another thread, which rolled it back (below);
- it was ended from inside one of its own operations, such as a pickle hook that calls the block's `__exit__`. That raises `RuntimeError` where it's called, and the transaction rolls back when that operation returns.

A commit that can't finish raises too: a busy or failed `COMMIT` raises `Timeout` or an `OSError`, and nothing is kept.

### Ending it from another thread

diskcache says a transaction "may not be shared between threads". In diskcache-oxide, any thread may call the transaction's `__exit__`, to commit (no exception) or roll back the owner's transaction. The rules:

- While the owner is inside one of its own operations (decoding a value, say), a rollback is left to that operation, and happens when it returns. A commit waits for it, up to the cache's `timeout`. A commit that can't run by then raises `Timeout` and rolls back.
- The owner's own exit afterwards raises `TransactionAborted` unless the transaction committed.
- An owner's exit that comes while the other thread is still committing waits for the outcome, up to the cache's `timeout`, and reports it. Past that, it raises `Timeout` ("whether it committed is unknown"). An exit with an exception passing doesn't wait.
- Writes the owner makes after another thread ended the transaction run on their own, outside it.

## `durable=True`

On a [`durable=True`](getting-started.qmd#a-cache-that-cant-take-a-request-down) cache, beginning a transaction still raises, and so does any failure inside the block: dropping one write and committing the rest would break the transaction's atomicity. Only calls outside a transaction are answered as misses.

## A transaction belongs to a thread, not a task

The calls that join a transaction are the ones made on the thread that entered the block. In asyncio, every task on a loop runs on that same thread. So if you `await` inside the block, another coroutine that runs meanwhile and writes to the same cache joins your transaction, and rolls back with it if your block raises. Don't `await` inside a `transact()` block. An `async with cache.transact_async()` form, where waiting for the write lock wouldn't block the event loop, is part of the planned `AsyncCache` experiment (see the [roadmap](roadmap.qmd)).

## Transactions and forks

A fork waits for every transaction other threads hold, with no timeout, so the child never inherits half of one (D-012). A long transaction holds up every fork in the process while it's open, and calls behind that fork time out (see [How long a call waits for a fork](concurrency-and-forks.qmd#how-long-a-call-waits-for-a-fork)). Forking from inside your own transaction can't be waited for: the child's copy is poisoned and raises `RuntimeError` (see [Forking from inside your own transaction](concurrency-and-forks.qmd#forking-from-inside-your-own-transaction)).

## Typing: `TransactionalCacheLike`

`Cache` and [`NullCache`](null-cache.qmd) both have `transact()`. Annotate with `TransactionalCacheLike` to accept either and call it:

```python
from diskcache_oxide import TransactionalCacheLike

def count(cache: TransactionalCacheLike, path: str) -> None:
    with cache.transact() as tx:
        tx.incr('requests')
        tx.incr(f'requests:{path}')
```

On a `NullCache`, `transact()` is a no-op that yields the `NullCache`. A [`FanoutCache`](fanoutcache.qmd) is not a `TransactionalCacheLike`: its `transact(*, key)` covers only the shard that `key` lives in, and refuses calls for keys on other shards inside the block. Annotate with `ShardedCacheLike` to accept a `FanoutCache` or a `NullCache`. `CacheLike` itself has no `transact()`, so a cache whose transactions need more than `retry=` (a sharded cache's `transact(key=...)`) can still be a `CacheLike`. A [`Caches`](caches.qmd) lookup is a `TransactionalCacheLike`, so `caches['general'].transact()` type-checks, and a disabled cache's `transact()` is the `NullCache` one.


### Coordination: locks, semaphores and throttles

A cache directory is shared by every process on the machine that opens it, and `add()`, `incr()` and `transact()` are atomic across all of them. That makes it a place to coordinate work as well as cache it: one worker at a time on a job, at most a few at once on a slow API, a rate limit every worker respects. diskcache-oxide ships diskcache's coordination recipes for that, under the same names.

```python
from diskcache_oxide import Cache, Lock, RLock, BoundedSemaphore, Averager, throttle, barrier

locks = Cache('/var/cache/my-app/locks', eviction_policy='none')
```

Two common jobs don't need a lock at all. When only one worker should run a job and the others should skip it, an `add()` claim is simpler: see [Running a job once across workers](../recipes/run-once.qmd). To hand work items to whichever worker is free, use a queue: see [Work queues](../recipes/work-queues.qmd).

## Lock

```python
lock = Lock(locks, 'report:nightly', expire=600)

with lock:
    build_the_report()
```

One holder at a time, in any thread of any process. `acquire()` waits, polling every millisecond, until it gets the lock; `release()` gives it back; `locked()` says whether anyone holds it. It isn't reentrant: the holder taking it again waits for itself. Give it an `expire`, so a holder that crashes without releasing doesn't keep the lock forever.

`RLock` is the reentrant one: the thread holding it may take it again, and must release it as many times. Its owner is the process and thread, with a per-process nonce, so another thread, another process, a forked child, or a container on the same volume that happens to have the same pid can never release or re-enter it. Releasing a lock you don't hold raises `AssertionError`.

## BoundedSemaphore

```python
api_slots = BoundedSemaphore(locks, 'api:partner', value=4)

with api_slots:
    call_the_partner_api()
```

At most `value` holders at once, everywhere. Releasing more times than it was acquired raises `AssertionError`.

## throttle

```python
@throttle(locks, count=10, seconds=1)
def send_webhook(event): ...
```

At most `count` calls every `seconds`, across every process: a token bucket stored under the function's qualified name (or `name=`). A call with no token waits until one is due. Two fixes over diskcache's: a bucket that expired or was cleared counts as full rather than raising `TypeError`, and decorating the function adds the bucket only if it isn't there, so every worker that imports the module doesn't refill it.

## barrier

```python
@barrier(locks, Lock)
def migrate(): ...
```

Runs the function under a lock made by the factory you pass (`Lock`, `RLock`, `BoundedSemaphore`, or your own), keyed by the function's qualified name: one caller at a time.

## Averager

```python
latency = Averager(locks, 'latency:checkout')
latency.add(0.080)
latency.add(0.120)
latency.get()  # 0.1
```

A running average whose total and count are updated together in one transaction, so every process adding to it agrees.

## memoize_stampede

`memoize_stampede(cache, expire)` is `memoize` with stampede protection: a result close to expiring is recomputed early, in a background thread, by one caller, while everyone else keeps getting the cached value. It's a cache, not a lock, so it works on a `NullCache` and a `durable=True` cache as `memoize` does. See [Caching expensive calls](../recipes/caching-expensive-calls.qmd#thundering-herds).

## Things to know

- **Use a cache of its own for coordination, with `eviction_policy='none'`.** Lock and semaphore keys are cache entries: least-recently-stored culling removes the oldest first, and a lock held a long time is old, so a full cache can evict a held lock. Under `'none'` nothing is ever evicted for size, only expired entries are removed, so give every lock an `expire`. `clear()` releases every lock in the cache, so keep other data out of it: `Cache('/var/cache/my-app/locks', eviction_policy='none')`.
- **Not on a `NullCache` or a `durable=True` cache.** The recipes refuse them with `TypeError`: with caching off every caller would hold the lock at once, and a durable cache could drop the `delete` that releases one, leaving it held forever.
- **Not while waiting inside your own transaction.** A recipe that would have to wait inside a `transact()` block on its own cache raises `RuntimeError`: waiting there holds the cache's write lock, so no other process could ever release the lock you're waiting for. Inside a transaction on a different cache, a contended recipe raises `TransactionBusy` at once rather than waiting ([D-030](divergences.qmd)).
- **On a `FanoutCache`** each recipe locks only its key's shard.
- `tag=` tags every entry a recipe writes, so `evict(tag)` releases them all at once. `barrier` passes it to the lock factory only when it isn't `None`.


### Concurrency and forks

A production Python web app is a crowd. Several worker processes, often several threads in each, a pre-forking server that creates and recycles those workers while they're busy, and a cron job or an admin script opening the same cache on the side. More and more, it's also free-threaded Python, where the threads really do run at the same time. diskcache-oxide is designed for all of that at once, and its test suite runs each of these cases on every change, because this is where cache bugs hide: not in `get` and `set`, but in what happens when two of them collide.

## Threads

One `Cache` can be shared by any number of threads. There's nothing to lock and no per-thread setup.

- **Free-threaded ready.** The extension declares `gil_used = false` and never relies on the GIL for correctness. Its shared state is guarded by Rust's own locks and atomics. Every change is tested on 3.14, 3.14t, 3.15 and 3.15t.
- **Waits don't hold up Python.** Anything that can wait, such as a busy write lock, reading a large value file, or a chunk of `clear()`, releases the interpreter while it waits, so other Python threads keep running on GIL builds too.
- **Threads queue fairly.** Writers in one process queue on an in-process lock for each database file instead of all retrying against SQLite's busy handler, and long maintenance calls like `clear()` and `expire()` step aside between chunks so a waiting write gets in.

### A bounded connection pool

diskcache opens a SQLite connection for every thread that touches the cache and keeps it. With 64 threads that's 131 open files in the cache directory, and a server with enough threads runs out of file descriptors.

diskcache-oxide shares a pool of connections per database file across every handle in the process:

```python
cache = Cache('/var/cache/my-app', max_connections=8)   # the default
```

The pool never holds more than `max_connections` connections, so at most `2 × max_connections + 1` files are open in the cache directory, however many threads you run. A thread that finds every connection busy waits for one, up to the cache's `timeout`. When the last handle on a directory closes, every connection closes with it, whichever threads used them.

## Processes

Any number of processes can open the same directory, each with its own `Cache`. That's the normal deployment: every gunicorn or uvicorn worker opens the cache at startup. A `Cache` or `FanoutCache` also pickles, so you can pass one to a `multiprocessing` or `ProcessPoolExecutor` worker: the copy reopens the same directory with the options the handle was opened with.

- **WAL mode, always.** SQLite runs in write-ahead-log mode, so readers never block writers and writers never block readers. One writer at a time commits to each database file. diskcache-oxide checks that WAL mode is really on when it opens a cache, and fails loudly if it isn't (on some network filesystems, for example).
- **Atomic across processes.** `add()`, `incr()`, `decr()` and every other write is a single transaction. Two processes can't both win an `add()`, and two `incr()` calls never lose an update. `pop()` is a read and then a transaction that deletes exactly the version it read, so two processes can't both get the same value.
- **Maintenance that doesn't destroy work.** Every write gets a new sequence number. `clear()` and `expire()` note the latest number when they start and only touch older rows, so writes from other processes that land while they run are kept.
- **Large values are always whole.** A process reading a large value while another overwrites it gets the old value or the new one, never a miss. (diskcache's standalone reproduction of that race sees about 40 misses in every 325,000 reads.)
- **One write lock per database file.** Every writer to a directory queues on its lock, so with many processes writing often a plain `Cache` stops scaling at a couple of processes. A [`FanoutCache`](fanoutcache.qmd) has one lock per shard and keeps scaling (5.7x a plain `Cache` at 8 processes on a 99:1 read/write mix). It doesn't change the thread picture below: threads sharing one handle on free-threaded Python are not lifted by it today.
- **Opening never writes.** Opening a cache with unchanged settings and reading from it never takes the write lock or touches the database file, so a read-mostly worker costs the writers nothing.

## Forks

This section is about macOS and Linux. Windows has no `fork()`: there `multiprocessing` starts every worker fresh, each opens its own handle, and nothing here applies.

Pre-forking servers (gunicorn, Celery's prefork pool, `multiprocessing` with the fork start method) create workers with `fork()`, which copies the whole process. Picture a thread halfway through a write at the instant the server forks. The child is a photocopy of the parent, SQLite's note that this process holds the write lock included. But only the forking thread exists in the child, so the thread that was going to release that lock isn't there. In diskcache, that child's first write waits for a ghost: it stalls for the full timeout (60 seconds by default). Under a busy read/write load, that hits 20-50% of forks.

diskcache-oxide prevents it with a **fork barrier**, a crossing guard installed when `diskcache_oxide` is imported. It stops traffic in a specific order:

1. **Before the fork,** the barrier waits for any write transactions already running in other threads to commit, and holds off new ones. It waits with the interpreter released, so the threads it waits for can finish. Then it closes the idle pooled connections, so the child doesn't inherit SQLite's lock bookkeeping for those files.
2. **In the parent,** it lets the held-off writes continue.
3. **In the child,** it drops any connection still inherited without closing it (closing a connection inherited across a fork is unsafe in SQLite), and opens fresh ones on first use.

The result: whatever other threads were doing at the moment of the fork, the child is born with no locks and no debts, and can read and write right away. The barrier covers every `Cache` in the process, not just the one you're holding. Your own `os.register_at_fork(after_in_child=...)` hooks can use a cache too, whether they were registered before or after `diskcache_oxide` was imported.

Closing the idle connections matters for more than file descriptors. SQLite keeps one lock record per database file per process, and a new connection that finds a record saying the process already holds a shared lock takes no lock of its own. A child that inherited such a record would run with no real locks, and once the parent closed its cache, another process's last close could delete the write-ahead log under the child and lose its writes. The cost is that the parent reopens connections after each fork.

The only connections a child can still inherit are the ones the forking thread itself was using: a transaction it holds (see below), or an operation it forked from inside, such as from a callback. The child leaves those file descriptors open by design.

### How long a call waits for a fork

A fork counts against `timeout`. A cache call behind a pending fork waits for it through the call's own `timeout` and then raises `Timeout`, so `timeout` has to exceed the work in flight, plus the fork, plus the interpreter hand-off. A fork takes about a millisecond in a quiet small process, but tens to hundreds of milliseconds beside busy threads on a GIL build (the forking thread has to get the interpreter back), longer in a large process, and it waits for work in flight such as a forced checkpoint. A `timeout` under that sees `Timeout` during ordinary forks, and a loop on `timeout=0` adds to the problem by being one of those busy threads.

A fork waits for every [transaction](transactions.qmd) another thread holds, with no timeout of its own, so a long transaction delays every fork in the process. Code that holds a transaction or runs inside a pickle hook (or a registered type's `decode` function, which runs in the same place), and waits for another thread's cache call, can keep a fork from finishing: the fork waits for that code, and the other thread waits for the fork. That other thread's call now raises `Timeout`, and the fork finishes once your code lets go. Until it does, `os.fork()` doesn't return, a second `os.fork()` queues behind it, and every thread with no transaction or hook of its own gets `Timeout` on every `Cache` in the process, after using up its whole `timeout` (60 seconds by default). Other processes aren't affected. If the code never reacts (a hook that retries forever, or one blocked on something that isn't a cache call), the fork stays stuck. A hook stuck in C code that holds the GIL stops everything, as it would without a cache.

Two calls don't raise. `checkpoint()` returns `False` when a fork keeps it from running. `close()` takes at most about 2 seconds behind a stuck fork, 1 for the checkpoint and 1 for the release, and `del` about 1, whatever `timeout` is. An ordinary fork ends well inside that, so `close()` waits it out as usual. If the fork outlasts it, `close()` returns anyway and the connections close when the fork ends.

Before-fork hooks run in reverse registration order, and `logging` and `concurrent.futures` each take a lock in theirs and keep it until the fork is over. `diskcache_oxide` makes sure its own hook runs before those two, so they stay usable while a fork waits for your code: a pickle hook or a `decode` function can still log or submit work. Two things it can't fix. Another library's hook that takes a lock and is registered after `diskcache_oxide` stays held while a fork is stuck. And a thread that calls the cache while holding `logging`'s module lock can hold up a fork until that call's `timeout`.

With [`durable=True`](getting-started.qmd#a-cache-that-cant-take-a-request-down), a `Timeout` behind a fork is a miss or `False` rather than an exception on a single-key call, so a `timeout` shorter than this makes ordinary forks into misses. A pickle hook or a registered type's `decode` that re-raises the `Timeout` it got from another thread's call lets go of its level under any policy, which clears the stuck fork. What `durable=True` adds is that the request doesn't fail: that `Timeout` is a miss, with the row kept.

### Forking from inside your own transaction

CPython won't let a library refuse a fork, so the barrier can't wait for a [transaction](transactions.qmd) held by the very thread that is forking. The child's copy of that transaction is poisoned: anything done inside it raises `RuntimeError` and nothing commits, and the child's writes to that database raise `RuntimeError` straight away instead of stalling for a minute. A `transact()` in the child doesn't join the inherited transaction either: it raises `RuntimeError` too. The parent's block carries on and commits as usual, and the parent gets a `RuntimeWarning`. A clear error at the call site beats a mysterious 60-second hang in a fresh worker.

## Free-threaded performance today

On free-threaded 3.14t, diskcache-oxide is already faster than diskcache at every thread count, and at a 1,000:1 read/write mix 8 threads reach about 1.4 million operations per second. But that's only about 1.6× its single-thread number, so threads don't scale the way they should yet. Profiling shows where the time goes: about 60% of a cached read is one system call SQLite makes to take its shared-memory read lock, under a process-wide mutex. Removing that wall is on the [roadmap](roadmap.qmd), after the Django backend. A [`FanoutCache`](fanoutcache.qmd) doesn't remove it for threads sharing one handle either; that is being worked on. See [Performance](performance.qmd).


### Storage and WAL

Nobody restarts a cache. It sits inside a worker process for weeks, and whatever it does to memory and disk, it does slowly and out of sight, until an alert fires at a bad hour. So how much a cache uses has to be something you set, not something you discover. This page covers what diskcache-oxide puts on disk, and the settings that keep memory and disk where you put them.

## What's in the directory

Open the directory and this is what you find:

```
/var/cache/my-app/
├── diskcache-oxide.sqlite        # keys, tags, settings and small values
├── diskcache-oxide.sqlite-wal    # SQLite's write-ahead log
├── diskcache-oxide.sqlite-shm    # SQLite's shared-memory index for the log
└── 3f/
    └── 3fa2…c91e.val             # one large value
```

A `FanoutCache` directory holds a small manifest file, `diskcache-oxide-fanout`, and one numbered folder per shard (`000`, `001`, ...), each laid out like the directory above.
